opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we debate constantly internally. My view, and the way we've organized our efforts at Google DeepMind, is that it's probably roughly fifty-fifty. About half of our effort goes into scaling, pushing the existing techniques as far as they'll go, and the other half goes into blue-sky research, the kinds of innovations that might be needed beyond that.

The reason I think about it that way is that scaling has clearly not run out of steam. We're still seeing very significant gains with each generation of models, maybe not the exponential jumps some people expected early on, but substantial returns. So it would be foolish not to push that hard. At a minimum, whatever the final AGI system looks like, I think these large foundation models will be a key component of it.

But I'm also fairly convinced that one or two more big breakthroughs are probably needed. Look at where today's systems are still lacking: consistency, what I sometimes call jagged intelligence, where a system can solve an Olympiad-level maths problem and then trip over something a child could do. True long-term planning, hierarchical reasoning, continual learning, the ability to come up with a genuinely new hypothesis or conjecture rather than just solving one someone has posed. Those feel like they may require new ideas, not just more compute and data.

So how do you assess it? Empirically, really. You look at the scaling curves, watch whether the capabilities you care about are moving with scale or staying flat, and that tells you where research is needed. And the nice thing is that the two are complementary. If you have the best scaled-up models, they become the platform for testing new ideas, and if you've got new ideas, you need scale to see whether they really matter. Historically, things like the Transformer, deep reinforcement learning, and AlphaGo came out of that combination of world-class engineering and real scientific innovation. I think the same will be true for the last few steps to AGI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's both, and the interesting question is really about the proportions and the timing. Scaling has been remarkable. Every time people have predicted that it would run out of steam, it's kept delivering, and I think we'd be foolish to bet against it in the near term. So part of what we do at Google DeepMind is make sure we're pushing scale as hard as anyone, because the empirical evidence says that works.

But my view, and I've held this for a long time, is that scaling alone probably doesn't get you all the way to AGI. If you look at the systems we have today, there are still clear gaps. They're not consistent. A system can solve an olympiad-level maths problem and then make a trivial error a schoolchild wouldn't make. That kind of jaggedness suggests something is missing, and I don't think you simply average it away with more data and more compute. Things like genuine planning, memory over long horizons, reasoning that's reliable rather than just plausible, understanding the physical world, and importantly, the ability to come up with a truly new idea or hypothesis rather than recombining what's already been seen. I think one or two of those will require real research breakthroughs, the sort of thing that in hindsight looks obvious, like the transformer or AlphaZero's self-play, but that nobody could have scaled their way into.

The way I assess it in practice is by looking at the curves. When a capability keeps improving smoothly with scale, that tells you the ingredients are there and you just need more of them. When you see a plateau, or you see that doubling compute buys you very little on a particular kind of task, that's a signal that you need something new. So we try to run a sort of portfolio, where a large part of the effort is on scaling and engineering, and then there's a significant chunk devoted to more exploratory, blue-sky research, where we're asking what the next AlphaGo moment looks like.

And the two feed each other. A new algorithmic idea is often only visible at scale, and scale without new ideas eventually becomes very inefficient. My guess, and it's only a guess, is that we're maybe a few breakthroughs away, not dozens, but not zero either, and that the timing of when those arrive is the biggest source of uncertainty in anyone's timelines, including mine.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s both, and the interesting question is how those two things interact. Scaling gives us a way to push existing ideas much further, but research determines how efficiently we can use that scale and what capabilities it can produce.

To assess that, I’d look at more than whether a bigger model gets a better benchmark score. Does it become more reliable? Can it solve unfamiliar problems? Can it plan over longer horizons and recognise when it’s made a mistake? You want to understand whether the weaknesses are steadily improving with scale or whether some seem to persist.

And you need controlled experiments. If a new method achieves the same performance with substantially less compute, that’s meaningful progress, even if it doesn’t immediately produce the most powerful model. You can then ask what happens when you scale that method up.

So I wouldn’t bet everything on either proposition. I’d keep pushing the systems we know how to build, while protecting space for research that challenges their assumptions. The next breakthrough may make scaling much more useful, and scaling may expose the very limitations that tell us which breakthrough we need.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s going to be both. Scaling is itself a way of exploring what these systems can do. You build a larger model, train it more effectively, and then ask: which capabilities improved, and where are the weaknesses still surprisingly persistent?

But I’d be careful about treating every weakness as evidence that you need a completely new paradigm. Sometimes you need better data, a better training objective, or more computation at inference time. Other times, there’s a missing idea—perhaps in how the system plans, learns from experience, or checks its own reasoning.

The way to distinguish those is experimentally. Can you predict the improvement you’ll get from additional scale? Does it carry over to genuinely new problems? If a capability keeps resisting improvement, that’s a good place to concentrate research.

So I don’t see scaling and breakthroughs as competing strategies. Research makes scaling more productive, and scaling gives you the experimental platform to discover what research you need next.
